This guidance applies to all central government departments and their ALBs when considering going to market for any consultancy services, and should be taken into account by local authorities and the wider public sector.

The Consultancy Playbook forms part of the Sourcing Playbook. As such, the principles, guidelines and rules of the Sourcing Playbook still apply and should be considered alongside the Consultancy Playbook where appropriate.

Consultancy is broadly defined as provision of advice to fill a knowledge gap. This can be to identify options and recommendations, or advice to assist with implementing solutions, and will be time limited. It will usually relate to business change or transformation, but can also focus on more technical, sector-specific expertise. The individuals (consultants) delivering the service (output) will operate outside of the client organisation’s structure and staffing establishment. Contracting authorities should also refer to the guidance in the Consultancy Playbook when procuring any type of external

workforce service, where relevant. This includes contingent labour, professional services and resource augmentation.

Extended workforce is an industry term which encompasses any temporary staff and volunteers, as well as workers who deliver contracted out services. Staff who are engaged on a permanent or fixed term contract are not part of the extended

workforce. All staff included in this definition will need relevant background checks and a determination of appropriate tax treatment.

Definitions, examples and a discussion of the characteristics of various extended workforce services can be found in Annex 1.

We recognise that there isn’t a one-size-fits-all approach to consultancy requirements.

As such, the principles outlined here shall be implemented by departments and their ALBs on a comply or explain basis and be applied by contracting authorities proportionately to the value, scope and duration of the engagement.

What is new?

Version 2.0 of the Consultancy Playbook built on the previous version, with refreshed and updated guidance on:

Types of extended workforce:

the Consultancy Playbook has shifted from focusing primarily on consultancy services, to providing more detailed guidance on other types of extended workforce, in Chapter 1 and Annex 1

Internal government resources:

the Consultancy Playbook now refers to various internal Civil Service teams which provide consultancy-style services, as well as teams who can assist the procurement of extended workforce

Artificial intelligence:

emerging technologies like artificial intelligence are increasingly changing the world of consultancy, and their role should be considered when choosing pricing models and addressed via the contracts’ terms and conditions

Consultancy and other extended workforce spend data:

extended workforce needs to be categorised and declared accurately, to drive transparency in how much government spends on different types of extended workforce services, and support ambitions to reduce unnecessary consultancy spend

Going to market:

the Playbook encourages civil servants to contact GCA PROSPER ahead of procuring any extended workforce requirements to leverage their expertise and support. See pages 15, 32 and 33 for further information on GCA PROSPER

Public sector case studies:

the document contains public sector case studies of success stories when procuring extended workforce requirements. See page 34 and the Knowledge and Skills: Generation, Transfer and Sharing Guidance Note for these case studies

Who is the Consultancy Playbook for?

The Consultancy Playbook is aimed at commercial, finance, project delivery, HR, policy and other professionals across public sector contracting authorities and industry responsible for commissioning or managing consultancy work in the public sector.

Experience has shown us that successful project delivery requires cross-functional working, bringing together seven different professional areas of expertise. The key is ensuring that we have joined-up teams with input from the right functions early in the process.

The figure below provides an analysis of the key stages mapped against functional groups. This should be considered a guide to support contracting authorities in implementing the Consultancy Playbook and may vary in different contracting authorities depending on their structure.

Ministers, permanent secretaries, accounting officers, commercial directors, project sponsors and senior responsible owners (SROs) will also find this Playbook useful when acting as decision makers or approvers, or when conducting checks within the capacity of scrutiny and assurance.

2. Knowledge

a) Contracting authorities should always consider what knowledge needs to be generated in order to achieve the desired outcomes. You should check to see if there are existing toolkits, methodologies, reports, case studies, or if a similar project has been undertaken in your department or across government.

b) Even if previous knowledge does not answer all requirements, organisations should be asking themselves whether work that has previously been undertaken and the related outputs can inform the project brief and rationale. See Chapter 3: Maximising Value Throughout and the Knowledge and Skills: Generation, Transfer and Sharing Guidance Note for more information on how to maximise knowledge reuse, generation and transfer in consultancy engagements.

3. Support from internal governmental resources

a) There are a range of internal government teams who can be commissioned by public sector organisations for support. Some examples of these include:

The Policy Insights Unit (PIU) works across government helping Civil Service teams tackle complex policy challenges. Launched in 2016 as the Open Innovation Team, the PIU has delivered over 150 projects for more than 30 government customers. It provides tailored, in-house, consultancy-style support across all stages of the policy cycle. For more information, contact enquiries@policyinsightsunit.gov.uk

The Evaluation Services Unit (ESU) delivers high-quality, affordable evaluation services across government. Launched in 2024, the team provides end-to-end evaluation support, from advice on scoping and design through to full delivery. The ESU works with all government departments and arm’s-length bodies, and partners closely with the Cabinet Office’s Evaluation Task Force. For more information, contact enquiries@evaluationservices.gov.uk

The Systems Insight Team (SIT) provides practical, accessible systems thinking support to help colleagues across government make better-informed decisions on complex issues. SIT offers sector-leading tools that help users explore how complex systems fit together, while its training builds confidence and capability for teams of all experience levels. For more information, contact enquiries@systemsinsightteam.gov.uk

Policy Lab is a multidisciplinary team working across central government and beyond to help policymakers tackle high-profile and sensitive challenges. Since 2014, the team has used people-centred, participatory and innovative approaches to generate new insights and ideas for policy. It collaborates with policy teams throughout the policy cycle – from early exploration and engagement through to sustained programmes, supporting shared understanding and more informed decision-making. It also delivers bespoke capability-building training and workshops. For more information, visit the Policy Lab blog or contact team@policylab.gov.uk

The Government School of Design works with public sector organisations to strengthen the organisational capability required to use design effectively. The school provides consultancy support to help leaders commission, integrate and sustain design across policy, services and delivery systems. Support may include capability diagnostics, leadership briefings and organisational development programmes that improve how organisations recruit, structure and sponsor design work, enabling design capability to contribute consistently to public value. For more information, visit their blog or contact andrew.knight@education.gov.uk

Innovation & Consultancy Services (ICS) is the main source of in-house consultancy for the Northern Ireland devolved government. It has a multi-disciplinary team that provides independent advice, insights and service improvement for public sector clients. For more information, visit their website or contact ics@finance-ni.gov.uk

Similarly to ICS, some government teams are only available to provide support within their individual organisations. Public sector organisations are advised to check internally for further information on these.

b) If contracting authorities still need to procure external resources, they should contact the GCA’s PROSPER service, who can assist them through the pre-procurement stage, by providing support on the following activities:

conducting landscape assessments of the contracting authority’s current spend, use and need of extended workforce

advising how to identify value, tracking and reporting on value realisation

suggesting compliant and best value GCA routes to market, including advice on appropriate delivery models and commercial aspects

providing best-practice guidance on contract management, and building departmental capability when procuring extended workforce

advising on how to become the customer of choice and getting maximum benefit from market engagement including SMEs

advising contracting authorities on planning for knowledge transfer as part of the contract

To get in touch, contact prosper@gca.gov.uk See pages 32 and 33 for further information on GCA PROSPER.

c) If contracting authorities need to procure an extended workforce service which may be highly complex or critical, they can contact the GCA’s Complex Transactions Team via CTTAccountManagement@gca.gov.uk for expert commercial support.

d) If possible and appropriate, contracting authorities may consider using an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool to address skills or capacity shortages. See pages 24 and 25 for further guidance on using AI in consultancy engagements, including sources like the AI Playbook and Digital, Data and Technology Playbook which can provide additional detail.

Where possible, you should undertake a proportionate level of market engagement for all procurements. Even for small engagements, some limited preliminary market engagement is likely to be a useful investment. Table 2 below shows a number of methods that you should consider. To support effective preliminary market engagement, departments should create and maintain pipelines of current and future contracts. This will allow suppliers to allocate their resources effectively, resulting in a more diverse range of bidders, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and voluntary, community, and social enterprises (VCSEs).

The Procurement Act 2023 (PA 23) mandates that prior to publishing a UK4 Tender Notice, contracting authorities must publish a UK2 Preliminary Market Engagement Notice if they plan to carry out preliminary market engagement for an above-threshold contract.

Further information on the notice types under PA 23 is available on Find a Tender.

When conducting preliminary market engagement, contracting authorities must take steps to ensure that suppliers participating aren’t at an unfair advantage, and that the competition isn’t distorted.

Table 2. Methods of market engagement

Method Benefit

Notification to the market of upcoming work - Allows contracting authorities time to prepare and suppliers to get a suitable bidding team together.

- Advisable for most procurements.

Expression of interest (EOI) - Highlights if there are no suitable or interested suppliers, allowing us to modify the tender if necessary.

- Filters the market based on capacity and interest for the requirement.

Request for information (RFI) - Allows suppliers to provide information that can inform the structure of the requirement. This can be of particular benefit if you don’t fully understand the outcomes you want to achieve.

- You can directly benefit from the expertise and experience of the market.

- Gives opportunity for suppliers to demonstrate innovation.

Supplier days/ webinars - Can passionately articulate the vision of the requirement to suppliers in a compliant way.

- Opportunity to request feedback from the market through Q&A.

- Ask open questions of the market, rather than seeking to confirm existing decisions ahead of releasing an Invitation to Tender (ITT).

- Can reduce the number of clarification questions during the tender process.

Consider SMEs and VCSEs: Market engagement

Ensure that you are engaging with a range of supplier profiles during market engagement activities, bearing in mind that smaller, lesser known suppliers may have access to the expertise you need.

Create, publish and maintain a pipeline of future and current contracts, allowing suppliers to allocate their resources effectively, resulting in a more diverse range of bidders.

PA 23 mandates that contracting authorities who will pay more than £100 million in certain contracts must publish a pipeline notice annually with details about any contracts with an estimated value over £2 million they intend to procure that year.

Off-payroll working rules (IR35)

The off-payroll working rules, also known as (IR35), ensure that a worker in the extended workforce broadly pays the same amount of Income Tax and National Insurance as an employee would.

Off-payroll working rules (IR35) can often apply to extended workforce engagements depending on the nature of the arrangements and the supply chain. Contracting authorities should introduce controls to ensure that they recognise where off-payroll working rules apply to their extended workforce contracts and then meet their requirements under the applicable legislation.

There is a greater risk of the rules applying where external staff are integrated within Civil Service teams, or where civil servants and consultants collaborate to deliver solutions or outcomes together.

IR35 should be considered on a case-by-case basis, and contracting authorities should take specialist advice via their own tax function, engaging the Tax Centre of Excellence (Tax CoE) or specific legal advice where necessary.

Refer to the Tax CoE guidance on consultancy arrangements and off-payroll working legislation to ensure that requirements under the legislation are understood. The Tax CoE website also provides relevant webinars regarding IR35.

The Tax CoE can be contacted for further support via govfinance@hmtreasury.gov.uk although departments are advised to contact their internal tax functions first.

Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in the world of consultancy. As a result, this could influence the following:

the structure of consultancies

the outputs delivered and how the service is delivered

the pricing models used to pay for consultancy services

the procurement process

the inclusion of terms and conditions which refer to the use of AI in consultancy engagements

As consultancies continue to embed AI in their operations, it is expected that the traditional “pyramid” consultancy model may change as AI systems automate certain tasks which are typically completed by junior consultants.

The inclusion of AI may positively impact the delivery of your requirements as it can develop innovative ways of addressing policy challenges. However, before including AI in a service, you should consider your organisation’s data maturity as AI relies on good data quality.

Cleaning and addressing unstructured data can be a painstaking and manual exercise.
